title: Stacks
summary: A collection where you only ever touch the top: last in, first out.
objectives: Explain **last in, first out** with an everyday example
Trace `push`, `pop` and `peek` on paper without mistakes
Say why push and pop are **O(1)** on an array-backed stack
Recognise the **call stack** and what a stack overflow is

steps.title: A pile of plates

state.caption: Only the top plate is easy to reach

steps.narration: Picture a pile of clean plates. You can't pull one from the middle without a crash. You only ever **add to the top** or **take from the top**. A stack in computing works exactly like this pile [S1].

steps.title: Adding a plate

state.caption: New plates always go on top

steps.narration: A freshly washed plate goes **on top** of the pile. Programmers call this **push**. Nothing underneath moves [S1].

steps.title: Taking a plate

state.caption: You get the newest plate back first

steps.narration: When you need a plate you take the **top** one, which is the one you added most recently. Programmers call this **pop** [S1].
whatChanged: - plate D popped off the top

steps.title: Last in, first out
steps.narration: The plate that went in **last** comes out **first**. That rule has a name: **LIFO**, last in, first out. Plate A, the first one in, will be the last one out.

callout.text: A queue is the opposite: first in, first out, like a line at a shop.

steps.title: You already use stacks

state.caption: Back takes you to the most recent page

steps.narration: Your browser's **Back** button behaves like a stack: each page you visit is pushed, and Back pops you to the most recent one. **Undo** in an editor works the same way, newest change first.

code.title: Python
code.src:
stack = []
stack.append(4)      # push 4
stack.append(6)      # push 6
stack.append(5)      # push 5
top = stack[-1]      # peek -> 5
stack.pop()          # pop  -> 5
stack.append(9)      # push 9
while stack:
    stack.pop()      # 9, 6, 4
stack.pop()          # IndexError!

steps.title: An empty stack
steps.narration: A stack starts **empty**. It has one door, the **top**, and every operation goes through it. In Python a plain list works as a stack [S2].

steps.title: push(4)
steps.narration: **push** adds an item to the top. The stack had nothing, so 4 lands at the bottom and is also the top [S1].

steps.title: push(6)
steps.narration: 6 goes **on top of** 4. Nothing below the top moves. In Python, `append()` is push: it adds to the end of the list, and the end is the top [S2].

steps.title: push(5)
steps.narration: One more push. The stack now holds 4, 6, 5 from bottom to top. Notice you can **see** 4 and 6 but you can't reach them without removing what's above [S1].

steps.title: peek(): look, don't touch
steps.narration: **peek** returns the top item **without removing it** [S1]. In Python you read `stack[-1]`. The size stays 3.

callout.text: peek is optional in the classic definition; push and pop are the two essential operations [S1].

steps.title: pop() → 5
steps.narration: **pop** removes the top item and hands it back. 5 was pushed **last**, so it comes out **first**: last in, first out [S1]. `pop()` with no index does this on a Python list [S2].

steps.title: push(9)
steps.narration: Pushes and pops can interleave freely. 9 goes on top of 6, taking the spot 5 just left.

steps.title: Pop until empty
steps.narration: Popping everything gives **9, 6, 4**: the reverse of the order they went in. Reversing order is the signature of a stack, and it's why stacks can reverse a word or undo edits.

steps.title: Pop on empty: underflow
steps.narration: There's nothing left to pop. Popping or peeking an empty stack is an **underflow** [S1]. Python raises `IndexError`, so check `if stack:` first.

callout.text: Always check for empty before pop or peek; this is the most common stack bug.

code.title: Array-backed stack (Python)

steps.title: The interface

state.note: Top lives at the END of the array

steps.narration: A stack is an **abstract data type**: it promises `push`, `pop` and usually `peek`, but not how they're stored [S1]. The common choice is an array where the **end is the top**, so no item ever shifts.

steps.title: push writes one slot

state.note: push: write at index size, size += 1

steps.narration: Push writes into the next free slot and bumps the size. No other slot is touched, so adding at the end of a dynamic array takes amortized **O(1)** time, however many items there are [S1].

steps.title: Full? Grow the array

state.note: Full array: copy into one twice as big

steps.narration: When the array is full, a dynamic array allocates a bigger one and copies everything. That copy is rare, so pushes are **amortized O(1)**: on average, constant time [S1].

callout.text: Doubling the capacity is what keeps the average cost constant: the expensive copies get further and further apart.

steps.title: pop reads the end
steps.narration: Pop checks for empty, then removes from the end. Removing from the end of a dynamic array takes amortized **O(1)** time [S1]. Removing from the *front* would shift every item, which is why the top is the end.

steps.title: Your programs run on a stack

state.note: Each call pushes a frame; each return pops one

steps.narration: The **call stack** stores information about the functions currently running [S3]. Calling a function pushes a frame; returning pops it. That's why the most recent call always finishes first.

code.title: Recursion

steps.title: Stack overflow

state.note: Too many frames: the stack runs out of room

steps.narration: The call stack has a limited amount of space. Recursion with no base case keeps pushing frames until it exceeds that bound: a **stack overflow**, which usually crashes the program [S4].

callout.text: Python guards this with a recursion limit and raises RecursionError instead of crashing.

code.title: No base case

quiz.q: You push 1, then 2, then 3. What does the next `pop()` return?
quiz.why: Last in, first out: 3 went in last, so it comes out first [S1].

quiz.q: What does `peek()` do to the stack?
quiz.why: peek returns the top item without modifying the stack [S1].

quiz.q: Push A, push B, pop, push C, pop, pop. In what order did items come out?
quiz.why: Pop takes B (top), C is pushed and popped next, then A is all that's left.

quiz.q: Why does an array-backed stack keep its top at the **end** of the array?
options: Ends never run out of room
quiz.why: Adding or removing at the end of a dynamic array is amortized O(1); at the front, every item would shift [S1].

quiz.q: What happens if you call `pop()` on an empty Python list?
quiz.why: Popping an empty stack is an underflow [S1]; Python signals it with IndexError, so check `if stack:` first.

quiz.q: A recursive function has no base case. What eventually happens?
quiz.why: Each call pushes a frame; with no base case the stack exceeds its bound: a stack overflow [S4].
